report.answer_text:
On April 2, 2025, President Trump announced a two-part "reciprocal" tariff plan under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). He called the day "Liberation Day."
1. Universal 10% baseline tariff
It applied to imports from all countries. It took effect at 12:01 AM EDT on April 5, 2025.
Goods already loaded on a vessel and in transit before that time were exempt.
2. Higher country-specific "reciprocal" tariffs
About 60 countries faced higher rates. These took effect April 9.
The administration said the rates were meant to be roughly half of the combined tariff and non-tariff barriers each country imposes on US exports. In practice they were tied to the size of the US trade deficit with each country.
The listed rates were meant to include the 10% baseline, not add to it. For example, China's 34% was the 10% baseline plus 24%.
Commonly cited rates included:
China: 34%
EU: 20%
Vietnam: 46%
Japan: 24%
India: 26%
Taiwan: 32%
Many other countries: 10%, including Brazil, Singapore, Australia and Argentina.
I'm giving the rates other than China's, and the 10% group, from memory. The sources I pulled confirm the China figure and the 10% countries.
Exceptions and related measures
Canada and Mexico were handled separately. USMCA-compliant goods stayed at 0%, and non-compliant goods faced 25%. Non-compliant energy and potash faced 10%.
The new tariffs sat on top of existing measures, including the earlier China tariffs. They did not replace them.
Separately, a 25% tariff on foreign-made autos and certain auto parts took effect around the same time.
What happened afterward
On April 9, the country-specific rates above 10% were paused for 90 days for most countries, leaving the 10% baseline in place. China was the exception, as tariffs between the US and China escalated further.
The legal basis was later challenged in court. Many of these details have changed since, so check current sources if you need the present rates.
Sources: Aprio, R.L. Jones, BGR, FreightRight
